and remain despised in the eyes of all.
And when she had killed them,
she dispelled indeed every fear,
and took the administration of the kingdom,
fulfilling her desires without fear.
And because the death of al-Hakim was thus kept hidden,
many believed that he had departed to the desert of Scete,
and had become a monk,
and had ended his life there.
Even I, the weak one, heard from Egyptian jurists,
when I was living in Damascus,
that at the time when al-Hakim was persecuting the Christians,
Christ our Lord revealed Himself to him, as to Paul.
And from then on he believed,
and departed secretly to the desert,
and died there.
And it is said
that this Caliph al-Hakim was only a little behind Pharaoh in pagan impiety.
For the latter used to say:
"The Nile is mine, and I have made it,"
as the prophet said.
And this one had certain men who would enter into his presence and say:
"Peace be to you,
O Single and Unique One!
Peace be to you,
O he who puts to death and brings to life,
and enriches and brings to poverty!"
And he would take pleasure in this.
And on this account, one of these flatterers of his,
when he went to Mecca
and entered their house of worship,
struck the Black Stone with a club that was in his hand and shattered it,
and said:
"Why do you worship and kiss,
O you who err,
that which neither benefits nor harms,
and have abandoned him who puts to death and brings to life in Egypt?" At this time, Abu Ali Hasan ibn al-Haytham of Basra, a skilled geometrician, became known.
About him, al-Hakim, the Caliph of Egypt, heard that he had said:
"If I were in Egypt,
I would perform on the river Nile a work that would be profitable to the high and low of that land."
And he sent and had him brought to him,
and honored him greatly,
and promised him lavish gifts,
so that he might also carry out that which he had spoken.
And when this Ibn al-Haytham went forth and traveled around the whole land of Egypt,
and saw the celestial likenesses that were most wondrously delineated there,
and the geometrical forms and marvelous figures,
he considered within himself and said:
"If there were any possibility of doing something further,
Abu'l-Hasan 210."
